title: CBSE Class 12 Business Studies · Practice paper 3
subject: Business Studies
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper contains 34 questions. All questions are compulsory.
Marks are indicated against each question.
Answers should be brief and to the point.
Answers to the questions carrying 3 marks may be from 50 to 75 words.
Answers to the questions carrying 4 marks may be about 150 words.
Answers to the questions carrying 6 marks may be about 200 words.
Attempt all parts of the questions together.

The board paper numbers the questions 1 to 34 without sections. Here they are grouped by marks:
Section A: questions 1 to 20 (1 mark each)
Section B: questions 21 to 24 (3 marks each)
Section C: questions 25 to 30 (4 marks each)
Section D: questions 31 to 34 (6 marks each)
There is an internal choice in questions 21, 23, 25, 28, 31 and 34, at the same places as in the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. Attempt only one of the alternatives in these questions.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Management is often compared with a profession. Which of the following features of a profession is fully satisfied by management?
options: Restricted entry through a prescribed degree or examination
A well-defined, systematic body of knowledge
A code of conduct that is legally binding on all managers
Compulsory membership of a professional association
questions.sol: Management has a systematic body of knowledge (principles and theories) that can be learnt. Entry into management is not restricted by any prescribed degree, membership of a body such as AIMA is not compulsory, and its code of conduct has no legal force. So only this feature is fully satisfied.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: In the store room of Lakshmi Engineering, every tool has a fixed rack with a label, and every store-keeper has a fixed counter. As a result, no time is wasted in searching for tools or people. Which principle of management given by Henri Fayol is being followed?
questions.sol: Fayol's principle of order means 'a place for everything (everyone) and everything (everyone) in its place'. It avoids loss of time and materials in searching.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Which of the following statements about delegation and decentralisation is correct?
options: Delegation is a compulsory act, whereas decentralisation is an optional policy decision.
Decentralisation is a narrow concept limited to a superior and his immediate subordinate.
Under delegation, accountability is also passed on to the subordinate.
Decentralisation means that all decisions are taken by top management.
questions.sol: No manager can do all the work alone, so delegation is compulsory. Decentralisation, the systematic delegation of authority to all levels, is an optional policy decision of top management. Delegation is the narrower concept; accountability cannot be delegated; taking all decisions at the top is centralisation.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Read the following statements carefully:
Statement I: Orientation means introducing the selected employee to other employees and familiarising him or her with the rules and policies of the organisation.
Statement II: Placement is the first step in the process of staffing.
Choose the correct option from the following:
options: Statement I is true and Statement II is false.
Statement II is true and Statement I is false.
questions.sol: Statement I is the NCERT meaning of orientation (induction), so it is true. Statement II is false: the staffing process begins with estimating manpower requirements; placement and orientation come after selection.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Navya Textiles arranges loans from banks, buys cotton from farmers' co-operatives, hires skilled weavers trained at local institutes and gets electricity from the state grid. It then sells its fabric to customers in the market. Which point of importance of the business environment does this highlight?
options: It helps in identifying threats and early warning signals.
It helps in coping with rapid changes.
It helps in tapping useful resources.
questions.sol: The environment is a source of the resources a business needs, such as finance, raw materials, labour and power; the business obtains them from the environment and supplies its output back to it. This is 'tapping useful resources'.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: After the managers of Pearl Jewellers began keeping a close check on the activities of the employees in the showroom and the store, cases of dishonest behaviour and pilferage fell sharply. Which point of importance of controlling is highlighted here?
questions.sol: Controlling creates an atmosphere of order and discipline in the organisation. It helps to minimise dishonest behaviour on the part of employees by keeping a close check on their activities.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: On a stock exchange, the share price of Asha Motors Ltd. rose after the company reported higher profits, and fell later when the demand for its shares declined. The exchange thus values securities on the basis of the forces of demand and supply. Which function of a stock exchange is highlighted here?
options: Providing liquidity and marketability to existing securities
questions.sol: Share prices on a stock exchange are determined by the forces of demand and supply, and the exchange is a mechanism for the constant valuation of securities. This is the function of pricing of securities.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Before buying an electric heater, Ritu checked that it carried the ISI mark. Which consumer responsibility did she fulfil?
options: Read labels carefully to know the price, net weight and expiry date
Ask for a cash memo on purchase of goods
File a complaint in an appropriate consumer forum
Buy only standardised goods, as they provide quality assurance
questions.sol: NCERT lists 'buy only standardised goods as they provide quality assurance': look for the ISI mark on electrical goods, the FPO mark on food products and the Hallmark on jewellery.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: At Mehra Tools, workers are selected scientifically, and each worker is given training that matches his or her abilities, so that each one can work at the highest efficiency and earn more. Which principle of Scientific Management is being followed?
options: Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity
questions.sol: Taylor's principle of development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity calls for scientific selection of workers and training suited to their abilities, which raises both efficiency and earnings.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Advertising is an impersonal form of communication.
Reason (R): In advertising, there is no direct face-to-face contact between the marketer and the prospective customers.
Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.sol: A is true: NCERT describes advertising as an impersonal form of communication, paid for by the marketer. R is true and explains A: the message reaches customers through media, without face-to-face contact, which is why it is impersonal.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: A pressure cooker bought by Neha burst because its safety valve was defective, and she was injured. She has filed a complaint, claiming that a consumer must be protected against goods that are hazardous to life and health. Which right of the consumer is she relying on?
questions.sol: The right to safety is the consumer's right to be protected against goods and services that are hazardous to life, health and property, such as a pressure cooker with a defective safety valve.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Trading on equity (using debt to increase earnings per share) will be favourable to the equity shareholders when:
options: the rate of interest on debt is higher than the return on investment
the return on investment is higher than the rate of interest on debt
the company has no debt in its capital structure
questions.sol: Trading on equity raises EPS only when the return on investment is higher than the cost (rate of interest) of debt; the extra return then goes to the equity shareholders.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: In the trading procedure at a stock exchange, an investor must open an account with a depository participant in which the shares bought are held in electronic form. This account is called a:
questions.sol: A dematerialised (demat) account, opened with a depository participant, holds securities in electronic form. Shares bought are credited to it and shares sold are debited from it.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Before the festival sale, the manager of Shopwell Stores prepared a plan stating clearly which department would do which work. As a result, no two departments did the same work and no resources were wasted. Which point of importance of planning is highlighted here?
options: Planning reduces overlapping and wasteful activities
questions.sol: Planning coordinates the activities of different departments, so that overlapping (two departments doing the same work) and wasteful activities are avoided.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Sunrise Industries Ltd. is a large, well-known company that can raise funds easily whenever it needs them. It therefore pays a high dividend to its shareholders. Which factor affecting the dividend decision is highlighted here?
questions.sol: A company with easy access to the capital market depends less on retained earnings, so it can pay a higher dividend.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Lotus Ltd. has registered its brand name 'Glow' and its logo under the law, so that no other firm can use them. A brand, or a part of a brand, that is given legal protection in this way is called a:
questions.sol: A brand or part of a brand that is given legal protection is called a trade mark; no other firm can use it. A brand mark is only the part of a brand that can be recognised but not spoken (a symbol or logo), a label carries information about the product, and a grade is a quality class.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Two banks have agreed to share each other's ATMs, so that each of them needs to install fewer machines. Which factor affecting the requirement of fixed capital is highlighted?
questions.sol: Sharing facilities with other organisations (level of collaboration) reduces the investment in fixed assets each one needs. NCERT gives the example of banks sharing ATMs.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: A tube of toothpaste is sold to customers in a printed cardboard box. The cardboard box is an example of:
questions.sol: Primary packaging is the product's immediate container (the tube). Secondary packaging is an additional layer of protection kept till the product is ready for use, such as the cardboard box. Transportation packaging is used for storage and transport, such as a carton holding many boxes.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Ravi Ltd. needs ₹20,00,000 for a new project. Plan I: issue equity shares of ₹10 each for the whole amount. Plan II: issue equity shares of ₹10 each for ₹10,00,000 and 12% debentures for ₹10,00,000. Its earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) are expected to be ₹2,00,000 and the tax rate is 30%. Which plan gives the higher earnings per share (EPS)?
options: Plan II, with EPS of ₹0.80 against ₹0.70 under Plan I
Plan I, with EPS of ₹0.70 against ₹0.56 under Plan II
Plan II, with EPS of ₹1.40 against ₹0.70 under Plan I
Both plans give the same EPS of ₹0.70
questions.sol: Plan I: EBT = ₹2,00,000; tax 30% = ₹60,000; EAT = ₹1,40,000; shares = 2,00,000; EPS = ₹0.70. Plan II: interest = 12% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹1,20,000; EBT = ₹80,000; tax = ₹24,000; EAT = ₹56,000; shares = 1,00,000; EPS = ₹0.56. The return on investment (2,00,000/20,00,000 = 10%) is lower than the rate of interest (12%), so using debt lowers the EPS. (₹0.80 ignores tax; ₹1.40 ignores interest.)

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: In a garment factory, the floor in-charge watches the work of the machine operators throughout the shift and gives them instructions on the spot, so that the day's target is met and materials are not wasted. Which element of directing is she performing?
questions.sol: Supervision means overseeing what is being done by subordinates and giving them instructions, to ensure optimum use of resources and achievement of work targets.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Distinguish between training and development on any three bases.
questions.model:
BasisTrainingDevelopment
1. MeaningA process of increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular jobA process of learning and growth of an employee in all respects
2. PurposeTo enhance the specific job skills of an employeeTo enhance the overall personality of an employee
3. OrientationJob-orientedCareer-oriented

points.t: Meaning: increasing knowledge and skills for a particular job / learning and growth in all respects
Purpose: specific job skills / overall personality
Orientation: job-oriented / career-oriented

or.text: State any three benefits of training to the employees.
or.model:
Benefits of training to the employees (any three):
1. Better career: improved skills and knowledge lead to a better career for the individual.
2. More earnings: increased performance helps the individual to earn more.
3. Fewer accidents: training makes the employee more efficient in handling machines, so he or she is less prone to accidents.
4. Higher satisfaction and morale: training increases the satisfaction and morale of employees.

points.t: First benefit to employees, with a brief statement
Second benefit to employees, with a brief statement
Third benefit to employees, with a brief statement

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Three managers of Vardhan Logistics lead their teams in different ways:
(i) Arjun takes all the decisions himself, gives orders and expects his team to obey them without question.
(ii) Bina discusses problems with her team, invites their suggestions and takes decisions after consulting them.
(iii) Charu lets her team set its own goals and decide how to do the work; she only supplies information and resources when asked.
Identify the style of leadership followed by each manager and state one feature of each style.
questions.model:
(i) Arjun: Autocratic (authoritarian) leadership. Feature: the leader gives orders, expects subordinates to obey and does not like to be contradicted; communication is one-way.
(ii) Bina: Democratic (participative) leadership. Feature: the leader develops action plans and takes decisions in consultation with subordinates and encourages them to participate.
(iii) Charu: Laissez faire (free-rein) leadership. Feature: the leader does not believe in the use of power; subordinates are given a high degree of independence to set their own goals and ways of working, and the leader supports them.

points.t: (i) Autocratic leadership identified
(i) One correct feature of autocratic leadership
(ii) Democratic leadership identified
(ii) One correct feature of democratic leadership
(iii) Laissez faire (free-rein) leadership identified
(iii) One correct feature of laissez faire leadership

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Explain the following factors affecting the working capital requirements of a company:
(a) Nature of business
(b) Operating efficiency
questions.model:
(a) Nature of business: The basic nature of a business influences the amount of working capital needed. A trading organisation usually needs a smaller amount of working capital than a manufacturing organisation, because there is usually no processing; the cycle from cash to inventory to cash is short. Service businesses, which hold little or no inventory, need still less.
(b) Operating efficiency: Firms manage their operations with different degrees of efficiency. Efficient management of inventory and debtors (better stock control, quicker collection from customers) reduces the amount of working capital needed; inefficiency increases it.

points.t: (a) Nature of business: heading
(a) Explanation: trading and service firms need less working capital than manufacturing firms
(b) Operating efficiency: heading
(b) Explanation: efficient management of inventory and debtors reduces working capital needs

or.text:
Explain the following factors affecting the investment (capital budgeting) decision of a company:
(a) Cash flows of the project
(b) The rate of return
(c) The investment criteria involved
or.model:
(a) Cash flows of the project: When a company takes an investment decision involving a huge amount, it expects to generate cash flows over a period. These cash flows are a series of cash receipts and payments over the life of the investment, and they should be carefully analysed before the decision is taken.
(b) The rate of return: The most important criterion is the return from the proposal. For example, if one project is expected to earn 10% and another 12% with the same risk, the second is preferred.
(c) The investment criteria involved: A decision to invest in a project involves many calculations about the amount of investment, interest rate, cash flows and rate of return. There are different techniques (capital budgeting techniques) to evaluate projects, and these are applied before a proposal is accepted.

points.t: (a) Cash flows of the project, explained
(b) The rate of return, explained
(c) The investment criteria involved, explained

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Vistara Hotels is opening a new wing with 80 rooms. Its HR Manager, Ms Kavita, took the following steps:
(i) She worked out how many housekeeping staff, receptionists and cooks the new wing would need, keeping in mind the work to be done and the staff already available.
(ii) She advertised the posts on job portals and contacted hotel management institutes, so that a large number of suitable candidates applied.
(iii) When the new staff joined, they were shown around the hotel, introduced to their colleagues and told about the hotel's rules and policies.
Identify the three steps of the staffing process described above.
questions.model:
(i) Estimating manpower requirements: finding out the number and type of people needed, through workload analysis (the work to be done) and workforce analysis (the people available).
(ii) Recruitment: searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs in the organisation.
(iii) Placement and orientation: placement is putting the selected person on the job for which he or she was selected; orientation is introducing the new employee to other employees and familiarising him or her with the rules and policies of the organisation.

points.t: (i) Estimating manpower requirements
(ii) Recruitment
(iii) Placement and orientation (orientation or induction accepted)

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Explain the following principles of management given by Henri Fayol:
(a) Unity of command
(b) Discipline
questions.model:
(a) Unity of command: There should be one and only one boss for every individual employee; an employee should receive orders from only one superior. If an employee gets orders from two superiors at the same time, authority is undermined, discipline is weakened, there is confusion about which order to follow, and order and stability are disturbed. So the dual subordination of an employee should be avoided.
(b) Discipline: Discipline is the obedience to organisational rules and the employment agreement that are necessary for the working of the organisation. According to Fayol, discipline requires good superiors at all levels, clear and fair agreements, and judicious application of penalties. For example, both workers and management should honour their commitments: workers should work to the agreed standards and management should pay the promised wages on time.

points.t: (a) Unity of command: heading / meaning (one boss for each employee)
(a) Explanation, with the effect of violating it
(b) Discipline: heading / meaning (obedience to rules and the employment agreement)
(b) Explanation (good superiors, clear and fair agreements, judicious penalties)

or.text:
Explain the following techniques of Scientific Management given by F.W. Taylor:
(a) Standardisation and simplification of work
(b) Method study
or.model:
(a) Standardisation and simplification of work: Standardisation means setting standards for every business activity, such as the process, raw materials, time, product, machinery, methods and working conditions. Its aims include making each process and product of a fixed type, quality and size, and establishing interchangeability of parts. Simplification means eliminating unnecessary diversity of products, such as varieties, sizes and dimensions. It saves the cost of labour, machines and tools, and leads to fuller use of equipment and higher turnover.
(b) Method study: The objective of method study is to find out the one best way of doing a job. There are various methods of doing a job; to find the best one, the whole process, from buying raw materials to delivering the final product, is studied using techniques such as process charts and operations research. The aim is to minimise the cost of production and maximise the quality and the satisfaction of the customer.

points.t: (a) Standardisation and simplification: heading / meaning
(a) Explanation (standards for activities; removing unnecessary diversity; benefits)
(b) Method study: heading / meaning (one best way of doing a job)
(b) Explanation (study of the whole process; process charts, operations research; lower cost, better quality)

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
The District Commission passed the following orders on four complaints filed under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019:
(i) A company was asked to give Mr Rao a new refrigerator, free from any defect, in place of the defective one he had bought.
(ii) A coaching institute was directed to return the full fee to a student, as the classes promised to her were never held.
(iii) A builder was ordered to pay a reasonable amount to a family for the loss and hardship they suffered because the flat was handed over two years late.
(iv) A soft drink company was directed to publish an advertisement to neutralise the effect of its misleading advertisement.
Identify the remedy available to the consumer in each of these cases.
questions.model:
(i) To replace the defective product with a new one, free from any defect.
(ii) To refund the price paid for the product, or the charges paid for the service.
(iii) To pay a reasonable amount of compensation for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party.
(iv) To issue a corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of a misleading advertisement.

points.t: (i) Replacement of the defective product
(ii) Refund of the price / charges paid for the service
(iii) Compensation for loss or injury suffered
(iv) Issue of corrective advertisement

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Explain any four points of importance of staffing.
questions.model:
Importance of staffing (any four):
1. Discovering and obtaining competent personnel: staffing helps in finding and getting competent people for the various jobs.
2. Higher performance: by putting the right person on the right job, it ensures better performance.
3. Continuous survival and growth: through succession planning for managers, it ensures the continuous survival and growth of the enterprise.
4. Optimum use of human resources: by avoiding overmanning, it prevents under-utilisation of personnel and high labour costs; at the same time it avoids disruption of work caused by shortage of staff.
5. Job satisfaction and morale: through fair reward for their contribution, it improves the job satisfaction and morale of employees.

points.t: First point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
First point: correct explanation of that heading
Second point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Second point: correct explanation of that heading
Third point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Third point: correct explanation of that heading
Fourth point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Fourth point: correct explanation of that heading

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Explain any four non-financial incentives that a manager can use to motivate employees.
questions.model:
Non-financial incentives (any four):
1. Status: the ranking of positions in the organisation. Higher status (authority, responsibility, perquisites) satisfies psychological, social and esteem needs.
2. Organisational climate: the characteristics that describe an organisation, such as individual autonomy, reward orientation and consideration for employees. A positive climate motivates employees.
3. Career advancement opportunity: opportunities for growth and promotion to higher levels, supported by suitable skill development programmes.
4. Job enrichment: designing jobs to include a greater variety of work content, a higher level of knowledge and skill, more autonomy and responsibility, and opportunity for personal growth.
5. Employee recognition programmes: acknowledging and appreciating good work, for example by displaying the names of the best performers or giving certificates.
6. Job security: some certainty about future income and work, so that employees do not worry about losing their jobs.
7. Employee participation: involving employees in decisions on issues related to them, for example through joint management committees.
8. Employee empowerment: giving more autonomy and power to subordinates, which makes them feel that their jobs are important.

points.t: First incentive: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
First incentive: correct explanation of that heading
Second incentive: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Second incentive: correct explanation of that heading
Third incentive: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Third incentive: correct explanation of that heading
Fourth incentive: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Fourth incentive: correct explanation of that heading

or.text: Explain any four points of importance of directing.
or.model:
Importance of directing (any four):
1. Directing initiates action: it is through directing that people start working to achieve the objectives of the organisation.
2. Directing integrates employees' efforts: every individual's work affects the work of others, so directing integrates the efforts of all the employees towards common goals.
3. Directing is a means of motivation: it guides employees to fully realise their potential and capabilities by motivating and providing effective leadership.
4. Directing facilitates the introduction of changes: people often resist change; through effective communication and motivation, directing helps employees accept the changes needed in the organisation.
5. Directing brings stability and balance: effective leadership, communication, supervision and motivation help to maintain stability and balance among the different parts of the organisation.

points.t: First point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
First point: correct explanation of that heading
Second point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Second point: correct explanation of that heading
Third point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Third point: correct explanation of that heading
Fourth point: correct heading (any one from the model answer)
Fourth point: correct explanation of that heading

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Swaad Foods Ltd. makes ready-to-eat snacks. Its Marketing Manager made the following observations about its business environment:
(i) 'The incomes of middle-class families have risen, so they are spending more on packaged food.'
(ii) 'People are becoming more conscious about health and fitness, and many prefer snacks made from millets and with less oil.'
(iii) 'New packaging machines can now keep snacks fresh for longer without adding preservatives.'
(iv) 'A stable government and peaceful conditions in the state have encouraged us to set up a new factory there.'
Identify the dimension of the business environment in each observation, quoting the relevant words.
questions.model:
(i) Economic environment: 'incomes of middle-class families have risen ... spending more' (income levels and spending power are economic factors).
(ii) Social environment: 'more conscious about health and fitness' (changing attitudes, values and lifestyles of people).
(iii) Technological environment: 'new packaging machines' (new methods and techniques of producing and packing goods).
(iv) Political environment: 'a stable government and peaceful conditions in the state' (political conditions, such as stability and peace in the country and the attitude of the government towards business).

points.t: (i) Economic environment identified
(i) Relevant words quoted
(ii) Social environment identified
(ii) Relevant words quoted
(iii) Technological environment identified
(iii) Relevant words quoted
(iv) Political environment identified
(iv) Relevant words quoted

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
When Mr Suresh Iyer became the Managing Director of Shree Cotton Mills, the company was making losses. Within three years:
(i) all the departments began working towards the same company targets instead of their own separate aims;
(ii) the cost of production fell, as resources were planned and used better and wastage was reduced;
(iii) the employees, who had earlier resisted new machines, accepted the new technology and adapted to the changing market;
(iv) the workers received better wages, training and opportunities to grow, and team spirit among them improved.
Identify the points of importance of management highlighted in (i) to (iv).
questions.model:
(i) Management helps in achieving group goals: it gives a common direction to the individual efforts of all departments towards the overall goals of the organisation.
(ii) Management increases efficiency: it aims to reduce costs and increase productivity through better planning, organising, directing, staffing and controlling of activities.
(iii) Management creates a dynamic organisation: it helps people adapt to changes in the environment, such as new technology, so that the organisation keeps its competitive edge.
(iv) Management helps in achieving personal objectives: through motivation and leadership, it helps individuals achieve personal goals (better rewards, growth, team spirit) while contributing to the organisation's objectives.

points.t: (i) Achieving group goals
(ii) Increases efficiency
(iii) Creates a dynamic organisation
(iv) Helps in achieving personal objectives

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Arogya Foods Ltd. is launching a millet-based breakfast cereal. Its marketing team took the following decisions:
(i) The cereal will contain no added sugar, will be sold in 250 g and 500 g packs under the brand name 'MilletMorn', and will be packed in a resealable pouch.
(ii) The 500 g pack will be sold at ₹180, after studying the cost of production and the prices of competing cereals; retailers will get a trade discount of 10%.
(iii) The cereal will be sold through supermarkets and online grocery platforms, and warehouses will be set up in four cities so that stock reaches the shops on time.
(iv) Customers will be informed through television and social media advertisements, and free sample packs will be given in housing societies.
Identify and explain the four elements of the marketing mix covered by these decisions.
questions.model:
(i) Product: Product means anything of value offered to the market for the purpose of exchange; it is a bundle of utilities that satisfies customers' needs. Product decisions cover features, quality, pack sizes, branding, packaging and labelling (no added sugar, 250 g and 500 g packs, brand name 'MilletMorn', resealable pouch).
(ii) Price: Price is the amount of money customers have to pay to obtain the product. Pricing decisions depend on factors such as the cost of the product, the demand and the prices of competitors, and include discounts and credit terms (₹180 per pack, 10% trade discount).
(iii) Place (physical distribution): Place covers the activities that make the product available to the target customers at the right place and time. It includes the choice of channels of distribution (supermarkets, online grocery platforms) and physical distribution such as warehousing, transportation, inventory control and order processing (warehouses in four cities).
(iv) Promotion: Promotion means informing customers about the product and persuading them to buy it. Its elements are advertising, personal selling, sales promotion and public relations (television and social media advertisements; free samples, which are a sales promotion).

points.t: (i) Product identified
(i) Product explained, linked to the case
(ii) Price identified
(ii) Price explained, linked to the case
(iii) Place / physical distribution identified
(iii) Place explained, linked to the case
(iv) Promotion identified
(iv) Promotion explained, linked to the case

or.text:
Describe the following factors that determine the price of a product:
(a) Pricing objectives
(b) Extent of competition
(c) Government and legal regulations
or.model:
(a) Pricing objectives: The price of a product is affected by what the firm wants to achieve through pricing. The objectives may be: (i) profit maximisation, in the short run (high price) or in the long run (lower price to build a large market); (ii) obtaining a larger market share, for which a low price is charged; (iii) surviving in a competitive market, for which the price may be reduced or a discount offered to clear stock; (iv) attaining product quality leadership, for which a higher price is charged to cover the cost of high quality and research.
(b) Extent of competition: When there is little or no competition, the firm has more freedom to fix a higher price, up to the upper limit set by demand. When there is free competition, the price is set close to the prices charged by competitors for similar products, near the lower limit set by cost.
(c) Government and legal regulations: To protect the public against unfair practices in pricing, the government can step in and regulate the prices of commodities, especially essential products such as medicines. It may declare a product an essential commodity and fix or cap its price.

points.t: (a) Pricing objectives: heading
(a) Explanation with objectives such as profit maximisation, market share, survival, quality leadership
(b) Extent of competition: heading
(b) Explanation: little competition allows a higher price; free competition keeps price near competitors' prices
(c) Government and legal regulations: heading
(c) Explanation: government may regulate prices to protect the public, e.g. essential commodities

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
An organisation was set up by the Government of India in 1988 to regulate and develop the securities market, and was given statutory powers in 1992. Among its activities are the following:
1. It registers and regulates stock brokers, sub-brokers, merchant bankers, underwriters and mutual funds.
2. It conducts training programmes for intermediaries of the securities market and carries out research on the market.
3. It promotes fair practices and a code of conduct for dealings in the securities market.
Answer the following questions:

parts.model: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI).

points.t: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) named

parts.q: (b) State any two objectives of this organisation.
parts.model:
Objectives of SEBI (any two):
1. To regulate stock exchanges and the securities industry, to promote their orderly functioning.
2. To protect the rights and interests of investors, particularly individual investors, and to guide and educate them.
3. To prevent trading malpractices and achieve a balance between self-regulation by the securities industry and its statutory regulation.
4. To regulate and develop a code of conduct and fair practices for intermediaries such as brokers and merchant bankers, with a view to making them competitive and professional.

points.t: First objective correctly stated
Second objective correctly stated

parts.q: (c) Identify the category of functions to which each of the activities 1, 2 and 3 belongs, and state one more function of each category.
parts.model:
1. Regulatory function. Another regulatory function: registration of collective investment schemes; regulation of takeover bids by companies; conducting inquiries and audits of stock exchanges and intermediaries; levying fees.
2. Development function. Another development function: undertaking measures to develop the capital market by adopting a flexible approach (for example, permitting internet trading through registered stock brokers).
3. Protective function. Another protective function: prohibiting fraudulent and unfair trade practices, such as misleading statements and price rigging; controlling insider trading and imposing penalties for it; undertaking steps for investor protection.

points.t: 1: Regulatory function
1: one more regulatory function
2: Development function
2: one more development function
3: Protective function
3: one more protective function

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text: Cosmo Consumer Ltd. makes three product lines: personal care products, packaged foods and home cleaning products. Each product line is run as a separate unit with its own production, marketing, finance and human resource heads. The head of each unit is responsible for the profit or loss of that unit. Last year the company added a fourth unit for baby care products without disturbing the existing units.

parts.q: (a) Identify the organisation structure adopted by Cosmo Consumer Ltd.
parts.model: Divisional structure (the organisation is divided into separate units, or divisions, on the basis of products, each with its own functional departments).

points.t: Divisional structure identified

parts.q: (b) Explain any three advantages of this structure.
parts.model:
Advantages of divisional structure (any three):
1. Development of managerial skills: product specialisation helps in the development of varied skills in a divisional head, which prepares him or her for higher positions.
2. Easy fixation of responsibility: each divisional head is accountable for the profit or loss of the division, so performance can be assessed easily and remedial action taken.
3. Flexibility and initiative: each division works as an autonomous unit, which leads to faster decision making.
4. Easy expansion and growth: new divisions can be added without disturbing the existing ones (as with the baby care unit).

points.t: First advantage, explained
Second advantage, explained
Third advantage, explained

parts.q: (c) State any two limitations of this structure.
parts.model:
Limitations (any two):
1. Conflict may arise among different divisions over the allocation of funds and other resources.
2. It may be costly, because each division has its own set of similar functions, so activities and resources are duplicated.
3. It gives managers the authority to supervise all activities of a division; in course of time a manager may gain too much power and ignore the interests of the organisation as a whole.

points.t: First limitation
Second limitation

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.text:
Swift Bikes Ltd. took the following steps while planning its growth:
(i) It decided to increase its market share from 10% to 15% within two years.
(ii) Its managers assumed that fuel prices would keep rising and that the government would continue its support for electric vehicles.
(iii) They listed three ways of reaching the target: launching an electric scooter, entering rural markets with a low-priced motorcycle, or buying a smaller rival company.
(iv) Each of the three ways was examined in terms of its cost, risk and likely returns.
(v) The electric scooter was finally chosen as the best way.
(vi) Production schedules were drawn up, resources were arranged and the sales team was given monthly targets.
Identify and explain the six steps of the planning process described above.
questions.model:
(i) Setting objectives: the first step is to set the objectives or goals to be achieved, stated clearly for the whole organisation (raise market share from 10% to 15% in two years).
(ii) Developing premises: planning is concerned with the future, so managers make assumptions about the future; these assumptions are called premises (rising fuel prices, continued government support).
(iii) Identifying alternative courses of action: once objectives are set and premises developed, the various ways of achieving the objectives are identified (three ways listed).
(iv) Evaluating alternative courses: the positive and negative aspects of each alternative are weighed in the light of their feasibility and consequences (cost, risk and returns examined).
(v) Selecting an alternative: the best plan, the most feasible, profitable and with the least negative consequences, is adopted (electric scooter chosen).
(vi) Implementing the plan: the plan is put into action; this involves the other managerial functions, such as organising resources and assigning work (production schedules, resources, sales targets).

points.t: (i) Setting objectives: identified and explained
(ii) Developing premises: identified and explained
(iii) Identifying alternative courses of action: identified and explained
(iv) Evaluating alternative courses: identified and explained
(v) Selecting an alternative: identified and explained
(vi) Implementing the plan: identified and explained

or.text:
Explain the following types of plans, giving one example of each:
(a) Method
(b) Programme
(c) Rule
or.model:
(a) Method: Methods provide the prescribed ways or manner in which a task has to be performed, considering the objective. They deal with a single task, which comprises one step of a procedure, and specify how this step is to be performed. Using an appropriate method saves time, money and effort and increases efficiency. Example: the method of training to be used for newly recruited supervisors (for instance, lectures and seminars) is different from that for workers (on-the-job training).
(b) Programme: Programmes are detailed statements about a project which outline the objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, human and physical resources required and the budget to implement any course of action. Example: a programme for opening a new branch, covering everything from the target date and funds to staff, premises and equipment.
(c) Rule: Rules are specific statements that tell what is to be done or not to be done. They do not allow for any flexibility or discretion, and they reflect a managerial decision that a certain action must or must not be taken. A penalty may be imposed for violating a rule. Example: 'Every worker must wear a safety helmet on the shop floor; a worker found without one will be fined ₹200'.

points.t: (a) Method: correct explanation
(a) Suitable example
(b) Programme: correct explanation
(b) Suitable example
(c) Rule: correct explanation
(c) Suitable example
